question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Restricted
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Copious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Restricted" means limited or kept within certain bounds; not free or open. (सीमित, प्रतिबंधित)

• Its antonym, "Copious", means plentiful, abundant, existing in large quantities, i.e. not limited at all. (प्रचुर, भरपूर)
◦ Example: She gave copious notes on the topic, leaving nothing restricted or held back.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Circumscribed (सीमित करना): Means restricted or confined within limits — a synonym, not an antonym, of "Restricted".

• Option 3: Capped: Means having an upper limit fixed on something — again a synonym of "Restricted", not its opposite.

• Option 4: Finite (सीमित): Means having limits or bounds; also a synonym of "Restricted", not an antonym.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Restricted": confined, limited, curbed, constrained.

• Other antonyms of "Restricted": unlimited, abundant, ample, boundless, unrestrained.

question:
Choose the option that is the correct indirect form of the sentence.
She said to her, "Please pay attention to the details."
option_1: She commanded her for paying attention to the details.
option_2: She requested her that to pay attention to the details.
option_3: She requests her that pay attention to the details.
option_4: She requested her to pay attention to the details.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. She requested her to pay attention to the details.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Reported Speech of Imperative Sentences with "Please": When the direct speech is a polite request beginning with "Please", the reporting verb "said to" is changed to "requested", the word "please" is dropped, and the imperative verb is converted into a "to + base verb" (infinitive) construction. The word "that" is NOT used with "requested" in this pattern.
◦ Structure: Subject + requested + Object + to + V1 + rest of the sentence.

• Applying the rule: "She said to her, 'Please pay attention to the details.'" becomes "She requested her to pay attention to the details."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "commanded" changes the tone of a polite request into an order, and "for paying" is an unnecessary and ungrammatical construction; "please" requests are never reported with "commanded".

• Option 2 is incorrect because "requested that to pay" mixes the "that-clause" pattern with the infinitive pattern — "that" should never be followed directly by "to + verb".

• Option 3 is incorrect for the same reason as Option 2, and additionally the reporting verb "requests" is wrongly kept in the present tense; it must be backshifted to "requested" since the reporting verb "said" is in the past tense.

NOTE

• Other reporting-verb changes for imperative sentences: an order → "ordered/commanded"; a request with "please"/"kindly" → "requested"; an advice → "advised"; all followed by object + to + V1, never by "that".

question:
Select the word that is similar in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below
Efficacy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Efficiency.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Efficacy" means the power or capacity to produce a desired result or intended effect. (प्रभावशीलता, सफलता से कार्य करने की क्षमता)
◦ Example: Doctors were confident about the efficacy of the new vaccine.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Efficiency", which means the ability to do something successfully with the least waste of time and effort, i.e. to be effective in producing results. (कार्यकुशलता)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Impotence (शक्तिहीनता): Means lack of power or strength — the opposite of efficacy.

• Option 3: Ineptness (अयोग्यता): Means lack of skill or the quality of being clumsy or incompetent — again nearly opposite to efficacy.

• Option 4: Futility (व्यर्थता): Means pointlessness or the state of having no useful result — opposite in sense to efficacy, which implies a result is achieved.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Efficacy": effectiveness, potency, success.

• Do not confuse "Efficacy" (effectiveness of a thing/treatment) with "Efficiency" (ability of a person/system to work without wasting resources) — in SSC synonym sets, efficiency is usually accepted as the nearest match to efficacy.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
All and sundry
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Everyone without distinction.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "All and sundry" means everyone, individually and collectively; every person without exception or distinction. (हर एक व्यक्ति, बिना किसी भेदभाव के)
◦ Example: The free food stall at the fair was open to all and sundry.

• The phrase combines "all" (everyone as a group) with "sundry" (an old word meaning "various, miscellaneous individuals"), together emphasising that no one is left out.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Advantages and disadvantages describes the idiom "pros and cons", not "all and sundry".

• Option 3: Full moon is unrelated in meaning; it does not correspond to any part of this idiom.

• Option 4: Holidays has no connection with the meaning of "all and sundry".

NOTE

• Other idioms meaning "everyone": "every Tom, Dick and Harry", "one and all".

• Do not confuse "all and sundry" with "few and far between", which means "rare, infrequent".

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Corruption is
P. misuse and abuse of public office, either directly
Q. typified by dishonesty, exploitation or the
R. or indirectly, for personal gains or unjust enrichment
S. in negation of due process or established protocol
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. QPRS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed opening phrase is "Corruption is", which needs a verb complement, so the sentence must continue with Q ("typified by dishonesty, exploitation or the"), since "is typified by" is the only grammatically complete continuation among the four parts.

• Part Q ends with "...exploitation or the", which needs a noun phrase to complete "the ___"; this is supplied by part P ("misuse and abuse of public office, either directly"), giving "...exploitation or the misuse and abuse of public office, either directly...".

• Part P ends with "either directly", which grammatically demands a following "or indirectly"; this is supplied by part R ("or indirectly, for personal gains or unjust enrichment").

• Part R ends with "unjust enrichment", which is logically and grammatically completed by part S ("in negation of due process or established protocol"), closing the sentence.

• Reconstructed sentence: "Corruption is typified by dishonesty, exploitation or the misuse and abuse of public office, either directly or indirectly, for personal gains or unjust enrichment in negation of due process or established protocol."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (PSRQ) is incorrect because it begins with P ("misuse and abuse...") right after "Corruption is", which is ungrammatical, and S does not logically follow P.

• Option 3 (RSPQ) is incorrect because it starts with R ("or indirectly..."), and a sentence cannot logically open with "or" immediately after "Corruption is".

• Option 4 (PQSR) is incorrect because placing P directly after "Corruption is" and then Q after P breaks the "either directly or indirectly" pairing, which must stay adjacent.

NOTE

• In para-jumble/sentence-rearrangement questions, first locate the part that grammatically fits right after the fixed opening (subject + verb), then trace connector words like "either...or", "the", and pronouns to link the remaining parts in sequence.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Fashion might not be first thing that comes to mind when we think of isolation strategies.
option_4: thing that comes to mind when
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Fashion might not be first.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence is: "Fashion might not be first thing that comes to mind when we think of isolation strategies."

• Rule — Use of the definite article "the" before a superlative-like ordinal expression: The phrase "the first thing" requires the definite article "the" before "first thing" because it refers to one specific, particular thing being singled out from all possible things that come to mind.

• The error lies in the segment "Fashion might not be first", which should correctly read "Fashion might not be the first".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "we think of isolation strategies." is grammatically correct as it stands — no article or verb error here.

• Option 2: "No error" is incorrect because an error does exist, as explained above (the missing article "the").

• Option 4: "thing that comes to mind when" is grammatically correct in itself and does not contain the error.

NOTE

• The definite article "the" is used before ordinal numbers/superlative-type expressions such as "the first", "the second", "the best", "the only" when referring to one specific item.

• Common SSC article-error patterns: missing "the" before superlatives and ordinals, unnecessary "the" before proper nouns, and missing "a/an" before a singular countable noun.

question:
Select the most appropriate 'one word' for the expression given below.
One who cures eye disease.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Ophthalmologist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Ophthalmologist" means a doctor who specialises in the diagnosis and treatment of eye diseases and disorders. (नेत्र रोग विशेषज्ञ)
◦ Example: She visited an ophthalmologist for her worsening eyesight.

• The word comes from the Greek "ophthalmos" (eye) + "-logist" (one who studies/treats), literally "one who studies/treats the eye".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Prologist is not a standard English word for a medical specialist; it does not mean "one who cures eye disease".

• Option 3: Phonologist (स्वर-विज्ञानी): A person who studies phonology, the system of sounds in a language — unrelated to eyes.

• Option 4: Biologist (जीव-विज्ञानी): A scientist who studies living organisms in general, not specifically eye disease.

NOTE

• Other common one-word medical specialists: Cardiologist (heart), Dermatologist (skin), Neurologist (nervous system), Orthopaedist (bones/joints), Otolaryngologist (ear, nose, throat), Pathologist (disease causes/effects).

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A person who is never happy with what he has
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Malcontent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Malcontent" means a person who is never satisfied and is always discontented or dissatisfied with their circumstances. (असंतुष्ट व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: The manager grew tired of the constant complaints of the office malcontent.

• The word is formed from the prefix "mal-" (bad/badly) + "content" (satisfied), literally "badly satisfied", i.e. never happy.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Heresy (धर्म-विरुद्ध मत): A belief or opinion that goes against accepted religious or official doctrine — unrelated to dissatisfaction.

• Option 3: Malleable (लचीला): Describes a person or metal that can easily be shaped, influenced, or persuaded — the opposite quality of stubborn dissatisfaction.

• Option 4: Miser (कंजूस): A person who hoards money and is unwilling to spend it, i.e. extremely stingy — not the same as being perpetually unhappy with what one has.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Malcontent" with "Miser"; a miser is defined by stinginess with money, while a malcontent is defined by chronic dissatisfaction, regardless of wealth.

• Other useful one-word substitutions with "mal-": Malefactor (a wrongdoer), Malapropism (comic misuse of a word).

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. BENIDICTION.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "BENEDICTION", not "BENIDICTION" — it means a blessing, especially a solemn one pronounced by a religious leader. (आशीर्वाद)

• Spelling key: BENE + DICTION. The root "bene-" (Latin for "well/good") is followed by "diction" (related to "speaking"), literally "speaking well/blessing". The option given wrongly changes the second vowel to "i" ("BENI-") instead of "e" ("BENE-").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "MOCKERY" is spelt correctly — it means ridicule or contemptuous imitation.

• Option 2: "CROCKERY" is spelt correctly — it refers to plates, cups, and dishes used at the table.

• Option 3: "RELIGIOUS" is spelt correctly — note the sequence "-gious", not "-geous".

NOTE

• Other Latin "bene-" words often tested for spelling: benevolent, beneficial, benefactor, benefit.

• Commonly confused vowel-swap spelling errors on SSC papers: e/i confusion as here, and a/e confusion (e.g. "seperate" vs. "separate").

question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. SABOTAGE.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "SABOTAGE" is the correctly spelt word among the given options — it means deliberate destruction, damage, or obstruction of something, especially for political or military advantage.

• Spelling key: SA + BO + TAGE. The word is of French origin and ends in the fixed suffix "-tage".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "MEALIGN" is incorrect; the correct spelling is "MALIGN" (to speak evil of someone).

• Option 2: "PRECISSION" is incorrect; the correct spelling is "PRECISION" — only one "S", not a double "SS".

• Option 4: "MISSIONERY" is incorrect; the correct spelling is "MISSIONARY" — the ending is "-ARY", not "-ERY".

NOTE

• Common double-letter spelling traps on SSC papers: PRECISION (one S), OCCASION (double C, single S), NECESSARY (one C, double S).

• Words ending in "-ARY" vs "-ERY": MISSIONARY, DICTIONARY, NECESSARY take "-ARY"; while BAKERY, GROCERY, MACHINERY take "-ERY" — these must be memorised individually as there is no universal rule.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Green light
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To permit something to proceed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Green light" means permission or authorisation to go ahead with a plan, project, or action. (किसी कार्य को आगे बढ़ाने की अनुमति)
◦ Example: The government finally gave the green light to the new highway project.

• The expression is drawn from traffic signals, where a green light signals that vehicles are permitted to move/proceed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To be lost and confused describes the idiom "to be at sea", not "green light".

• Option 2: To misunderstand describes the idiom "to get hold of the wrong end of the stick", not "green light".

• Option 4: To always compare does not correspond to any standard idiom involving "green light".

NOTE

• Other traffic-signal-based idioms: "red flag" (a warning sign of a problem), "to put the brakes on something" (to slow down or stop an action).

• Related permission idioms: "to give the go-ahead", "to give one's blessing".

question:
Some parts of a few sentences have been jumbled up, and labelled A, B, C and D. Select the option that gives the correct sequence in which these parts can be rearranged to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence
Our twelve years in the forest were
A. Ram had lost, we would have to
B. ending. Now, according to the wager
C. discovered our whereabouts, we would have to endure another ten years in exile
D. spend a year in hiding.
If during this year Mohan
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. BADC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed opening is "Our twelve years in the forest were", which needs a present/past participle to complete the verb "were"; this is supplied by part B ("ending. Now, according to the wager"), giving "...were ending. Now, according to the wager...".

• Part B ends with "the wager", which needs a subject-verb to explain whose wager; this is supplied by part A ("Ram had lost, we would have to"), giving "...according to the wager Ram had lost, we would have to...".

• Part A ends with "we would have to", which needs an infinitive verb phrase to complete the obligation; this is supplied by part D ("spend a year in hiding."), giving "...we would have to spend a year in hiding."

• The sentence then continues with the fixed closing phrase "If during this year Mohan", which is logically and grammatically completed by part C ("discovered our whereabouts, we would have to endure another ten years in exile").

• Reconstructed sentence: "Our twelve years in the forest were ending. Now, according to the wager Ram had lost, we would have to spend a year in hiding. If during this year Mohan discovered our whereabouts, we would have to endure another ten years in exile."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (BDCA) is incorrect because it places D directly after B, breaking the required link between B ("the wager") and A ("Ram had lost"), which must explain whose wager it was.

• Option 2 (CDAB) is incorrect because it starts with C ("discovered our whereabouts...") right after the opening fixed phrase, which makes no grammatical sense.

• Option 4 (ACBD) is incorrect because it opens with A ("Ram had lost...") directly after the fixed phrase, again producing an ungrammatical, meaningless sentence.

NOTE

• In such rearrangement questions, always check which movable part correctly completes the verb or connector immediately following the fixed opening phrase, then trace pronouns ("the wager"→"Ram had lost") and conjunctions ("If...Mohan"→"discovered") to link the rest logically.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
A fully grow Chihuahua weighs less than the average house cat.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. fully grown.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Past Participle as Adjective: When a verb form is used before a noun to describe a completed state or quality, the past participle (V3) form must be used, not the base form. Here, "grow" (V1) is used to describe the Chihuahua's state of having completed growth, so it must be changed to its past participle, "grown" (V3 of "grow").

• The adverb "fully" correctly modifies the adjective "grown", giving the standard phrase "fully grown", meaning "having reached full/adult size".

• Corrected sentence: "A fully grown Chihuahua weighs less than the average house cat."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "fullest grown" is incorrect because "fullest" is a superlative form of the adjective "full" and cannot be used as an adverb modifying "grown".

• Option 2: "fully growth" is incorrect because "growth" is a noun, and a noun cannot function as an adjective describing the Chihuahua directly after the article "A".

• Option 3: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original phrase "fully grow" is grammatically wrong, as explained above — an improvement is definitely needed.

NOTE

• Verb forms: grow (V1) – grew (V2) – grown (V3). Other common V1-V3 confusions tested by SSC: break-broken, choose-chosen, speak-spoken, write-written.

• The pattern "fully + past participle" is common in English: fully cooked, fully qualified, fully equipped, fully trained.

question:
Select the option that will improve the (bracketed) part of the sentence. In case of no improvement select the option 'No improvement'.
The play was (either as funny or as) disturbing as Shivang told it was.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. neither as funny nor as.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Correlative Conjunction "neither...nor": When two negative alternatives are being compared, English uses the fixed correlative pair "neither...nor", never "either...or" in a negative sense, and never "neither...or".

• Here, the sentence expresses that the play possessed neither the quality of being funny nor the quality of being disturbing to the extent claimed, so the bracketed part must read "neither as funny nor as".

• Corrected sentence: "The play was neither as funny nor as disturbing as Shivang told it was."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original bracketed phrase "either as funny or as" is grammatically wrong in this negative context.

• Option 3: "either as funny nor as" is incorrect because it wrongly mixes "either" with "nor" — the two words belonging to different correlative pairs ("either...or" and "neither...nor") cannot be combined.

• Option 4: "neither as funny or as" is incorrect because it wrongly mixes "neither" with "or" instead of the required pair "neither...nor".

NOTE

• Correlative conjunction pairs commonly tested by SSC: either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also, both...and, whether...or. These words must always be used strictly in their fixed pairs and never mixed with each other.

question:
Select the word that is closest in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below.
BLASPHEMOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. DISRESPECTFUL.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "BLASPHEMOUS" means showing contempt or lack of reverence for God or sacred things; profanely irreverent. (ईशनिंदा से संबंधित, अपवित्र)
◦ Example: His blasphemous remarks about the sacred text angered the devotees.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "DISRESPECTFUL", which means showing a lack of respect or courtesy towards someone or something regarded as important or sacred. (अनादरपूर्ण)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: COSTLY (महंगा): Means expensive — unrelated in meaning to "blasphemous".

• Option 3: REALITY (वास्तविकता): Means the state of things as they actually exist — unrelated to irreverence.

• Option 4: AUTHENTIC (प्रामाणिक): Means genuine or of undisputed origin — in fact nearly opposite in tone to something irreverent or false.

NOTE

• Other words related to irreverence: profane, sacrilegious, impious, irreverent.

• Antonyms of "Blasphemous": reverent, devout, pious, respectful.

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
He writes a paper every weekend.
option_1: A paper is written by him every weekend.
option_2: A paper is been written by him every weekend.
option_3: A paper was been written by him every weekend.
option_4: A paper was written by him every weekend.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A paper is written by him every weekend.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "He writes a paper every weekend" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V1/V5 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "a paper" becomes the subject (singular), so the auxiliary used is "is"; the verb "writes" becomes the past participle "written"; and "he" becomes the agent "him" with "by".
◦ Passive: A paper is written by him every weekend.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "is been written" is not a standard passive form — "been" has no place in the simple present passive.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "was been written" is doubly wrong — it mixes the past tense auxiliary "was" with "been", a form that does not exist in standard passive voice.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "was written" is the passive form of the Simple Past Tense, but the original sentence is in the Simple Present Tense.

NOTE

• Passive voice auxiliaries by tense: Simple Present → is/am/are; Simple Past → was/were; Present Continuous → is/am/are being; Present Perfect → has/have been.

• A sentence in the passive voice can never contain "been" immediately after "is/am/are" without "being" — "is been" and "was been" are always incorrect forms.

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
It is important to ensure that we all have good clean water to drink that is not ______ by heavy metals or chemicals.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. contaminated.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires a word describing water being made impure or unsafe "by heavy metals or chemicals". The word "contaminated" means made impure or poisonous by the addition of a harmful substance, which fits perfectly with the idea of heavy metals/chemicals polluting water.

• The structure "water...that is not ______ by heavy metals or chemicals" logically means the water should be free from pollution, so the blank must express "polluted/contaminated", negated by "not", to convey that the water is clean and safe.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "knotted" means tied in a knot — meaningless in the context of water quality.

• Option 2: "clarified" means made clear or pure; using "not clarified" would wrongly suggest the water should remain unclear, which contradicts the intended sense.

• Option 3: "purged" means cleansed or purified of something; "not purged" would again wrongly suggest the water should still contain impurities.

NOTE

• In fill-in-the-blank questions with a negative ("not ______"), always substitute each option into the sentence and check whether the resulting meaning is logical, not just grammatically possible.

• Related words: pollute, taint, adulterate (near-synonyms of "contaminate"); purify, cleanse, decontaminate (its antonyms).

question:
Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the part that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
They know they will face / either a swift backlash / or deafening silence.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence is: "They know they will face / either a swift backlash / or deafening silence."

• Rule — Correlative Conjunction "either...or": The pair "either...or" must join two grammatically parallel elements. Here, "a swift backlash" and "deafening silence" are both noun phrases, correctly balanced on either side of "either...or".

• The subject-verb agreement ("They know"), the future tense ("will face"), and the parallel structure are all correct, so the sentence contains no grammatical error.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "They know they will face" is grammatically correct — plural subject "They" correctly takes "know", and the future tense "will face" is properly formed.

• Option 3: "or deafening silence." is grammatically correct — a well-formed noun phrase correctly completing the "either...or" structure.

• Option 4: "either a swift backlash" is grammatically correct — a properly formed noun phrase that opens the correlative pair correctly.

NOTE

• When checking "either...or" and "neither...nor" sentences for errors, confirm that the two joined elements are of the same grammatical category (both nouns, both verb phrases, or both clauses) — a mismatch here is the most common error SSC tests.

• Also verify subject-verb agreement is governed by the noun/pronoun nearest to the verb in such correlative structures.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Jarred
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Altercated.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Jarred" (verb) means to have a harsh, jolting, or clashing effect; to be in conflict or disagreement with someone/something. (टकराना, विरोध में होना)
◦ Example: His careless remark jarred with the solemn mood of the meeting.

• Its closest match among the options is "Altercated", meaning had a noisy argument or heated dispute with someone, which reflects the sense of clashing/conflict carried by "jarred". (कहा-सुनी करना, बहस करना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Assented (सहमत होना): Means agreed or gave consent — nearly opposite to the clashing sense of "jarred".

• Option 2: Accorded (प्रदान करना/सहमत होना): Means granted or was in agreement/harmony with — again close to the opposite of "jarred".

• Option 3: Macho (मर्दाना): Describes a person showing aggressive pride in their masculinity — unrelated in meaning to the verb "jarred".

NOTE

• "Jarred" can also mean a physical, jolting impact (e.g. "The fall jarred his shoulder") — in vocabulary questions, the figurative sense of clash/conflict is usually the one tested.

• Other words meaning "clash/conflict": clash, conflict, wrangle, quarrel, dispute.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
This has given rise to the view that the legal code is __________ against women and the poor.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. biased.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes a "view" that the legal code unfairly favours one side "against women and the poor". The word "biased" means showing an unfair preference or prejudice for or against a particular person or group, which exactly matches the sense of unfair treatment described.

• The phrase "biased against" is a standard collocation meaning "prejudiced/unfair towards", making it the most contextually appropriate choice.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "baked" means cooked in an oven — meaningless in this context of legal fairness.

• Option 2: "frank" means open and honest in speech — does not fit the idea of the legal code being unfair "against" a group; "frank against" is not idiomatic.

• Option 4: "duplicitous" means deceitful or two-faced in behaviour; while negative, it describes dishonesty rather than unfair favouritism, and does not naturally collocate with "against" in this context.

NOTE

• The collocation "biased against/towards" is frequently tested in SSC fill-in-the-blank questions.

• Related words: prejudiced, partial, discriminatory (synonyms of "biased"); impartial, unbiased, neutral, fair (antonyms).

question:
Comprehension:

In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.
There were other stories (1) ________ Krishna. How (2) ________ been born in a dungeon where his uncle Kamsa had imprisoned his parents with the intention of killing him at birth. How, in spite of the many prison guards, he had been miraculously spirited (3) ________ to safety in Gokul. How, in infancy, he killed a (4) ________ who tried to poison him with her breast milk. How he lifted up Mount Govardhan to shelter his people from a (5) ________ that would have drowned them.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. about.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank follows the noun "stories" and precedes the proper noun "Krishna"; the sentence means "there were other stories on the subject of/concerning Krishna".

• Rule — Preposition of Topic/Subject Matter: The preposition "about" is used after nouns like "story", "book", "talk", "information" to indicate the subject or topic being discussed, i.e. "a story about someone/something".

• Applying the rule: "There were other stories about Krishna." is the natural, idiomatic construction.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "upon" is used to mean "on top of" or in fixed phrases (e.g. "once upon a time"); "stories upon Krishna" is not idiomatic.

• Option 3: "with respect" is incomplete on its own; the full idiomatic phrase would need to be "with respect to", which is not the natural collocation with "stories".

• Option 4: "belonging to" would imply ownership (stories that Krishna owns), which distorts the intended meaning of stories concerning/about Krishna.

NOTE

• Common "topic" prepositions: stories/books/talk about something, information/details about someone.

• "With respect to" and "with regard to" are correct only when used in their full form, not as "with respect" alone.

question:
Comprehension:

In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.
There were other stories (1) ________ Krishna. How (2) ________ been born in a dungeon where his uncle Kamsa had imprisoned his parents with the intention of killing him at birth. How, in spite of the many prison guards, he had been miraculously spirited (3) ________ to safety in Gokul. How, in infancy, he killed a (4) ________ who tried to poison him with her breast milk. How he lifted up Mount Govardhan to shelter his people from a (5) ________ that would have drowned them.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. he had.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "How (2) ________ been born in a dungeon where his uncle Kamsa had imprisoned his parents..." The passage narrates past events viewed from a later point in the past (Kamsa "had imprisoned" his parents before Krishna's birth), which requires the Past Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Past Perfect Tense: Structure: Subject + had + V3 (past participle). It is used for an action completed before another past action/point in time — here, the birth ("been born") had already happened before the narration point, and is further linked to the still earlier imprisonment.

• Applying the rule: "How he had been born in a dungeon..." correctly uses "had" with the passive past participle construction "been born".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "he have" is incorrect because "have" does not agree with the singular third-person subject "he" (it should be "has" in the present perfect), and in any case the present perfect is the wrong tense for this past narrative.

• Option 2: "he was" is incorrect because "was been born" is not a valid English construction — "was" cannot combine with "been" in this way.

• Option 3: "he has" is incorrect because the Present Perfect Tense ("has been born") does not fit a narrative entirely set in the past, which requires the Past Perfect "had been born".

NOTE

• The Past Perfect Tense ("had + V3") is commonly used in narrative/story passages to describe an event that occurred before another past event already mentioned.

• Do not confuse "was been" (always incorrect) with "had been" (correct passive past perfect construction).

How he lifted up Mount Govardhan to shelter his people from a (5) ________ that would have drowned them.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. away.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...he had been miraculously spirited (3) ________ to safety in Gokul."

• Rule — Phrasal Verb "spirit away": The phrasal verb "to spirit away/off" means to remove or convey someone secretly and swiftly, especially to safety, exactly matching the context of the infant Krishna being secretly carried to safety in Gokul.

• Applying the rule: "...he had been miraculously spirited away to safety in Gokul." is the correct, idiomatic phrasal verb usage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "around" does not form a recognised phrasal verb with "spirited" in this sense; "spirited around" is not idiomatic.

• Option 3: "together" does not combine with "spirited" to form any standard phrasal verb.

• Option 4: "gone" is grammatically impossible here since the blank must pair with "spirited" as a single phrasal verb, and "spirited gone" is not valid English.

NOTE

• Other common phrasal verbs with "away": run away (flee), give away (reveal/donate), take away (remove), pass away (die).

• "Spirit away" is often tested in cloze passages describing rescues or secret escapes.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. demoness.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...he killed a (4) ________ who tried to poison him with her breast milk."

• The relative pronoun "who" is followed later in the sentence by the possessive pronoun "her", which explicitly indicates the missing noun refers to a female being.

• Among the options, only "demoness" is a feminine noun (referring, in this legend, to the demoness Putana, who tried to kill the infant Krishna with poisoned breast milk), matching the pronoun "her" used later in the same sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "god" is grammatically inconsistent because it is not gender-marked as female, and cannot correctly be followed by the feminine pronoun "her".

• Option 2: "demon" is the masculine form and, like "god", does not agree with the feminine pronoun "her" used later to refer back to the same subject.

• Option 3: "satan" refers to a specific singular figure from Abrahamic tradition, is conventionally treated as masculine, and does not agree with "her"; it is also contextually unrelated to the Krishna legend.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always check pronoun agreement (he/she/it, his/her/its) later in the sentence to confirm the gender of the missing noun.

• This detail refers to the mythological episode of Putana, a demoness sent to poison the infant Krishna with her breast milk.

How he lifted up Mount Govardhan to shelter his people from a (5) ________ that would have drowned them.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. deluge.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "How he lifted up Mount Govardhan to shelter his people from a (5) ________ that would have drowned them."

• The key clue is the phrase "that would have drowned them", which requires a noun denoting a large body of water or flood-like event capable of drowning people.

• "Deluge" means a severe flood; a great overflowing of water, which precisely matches an event that could "drown" people and from which shelter (holding up a mountain) would be needed. (This refers to the mythological episode of Krishna lifting Mount Govardhan to shelter people from torrential rain sent by Indra.)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "snowfall" cannot logically "drown" people; snow does not fit the verb "drowned".

• Option 2: "earthquake" is a seismic event, not a water-based one, and people are not typically described as being "drowned" by an earthquake.

• Option 3: "drought" refers to a prolonged shortage of water, which is the opposite of an event that would drown people.

NOTE

• When choosing an answer in a cloze passage, always match the missing word to nearby verbs/clues in the sentence ("drowned" here clearly signals a water-related noun).

• Other water-related nouns often tested: flood, torrent, downpour, inundation (all near-synonyms of "deluge").
